stages.name: Economies and diseconomies of scale
stages.title: Economies and diseconomies of scale
stages.sub: How average costs change as a firm changes the size of its whole operation.

steps.q: A bakery wants to double its ovens, vans and staff, not just run its one kitchen harder. Is a fixed factory size still a limit on this plan?
steps.right: No, every factor can be changed
steps.wrong: Yes, the building size still limits it
steps.hint: Think about which period allows every input, including buildings, to be altered.
steps.pre: When every factor of production can be varied, the firm is planning in

steps.q: For each possible factory size the firm could build, there is a lowest average cost it could achieve at that size. If you joined up the lowest achievable average cost at every possible size, what would you be plotting?
steps.right: The lowest average cost for every size of operation
steps.wrong: The lowest average cost for one fixed factory only
steps.hint: This is about comparing many different sizes, not sticking with one.
steps.pre: That curve, showing the lowest average cost at each output when the firm can choose any size, is the

steps.q: Once the bakery actually builds a factory of a chosen size, some costs (like the building) become fixed for a while. Does the average cost curve for that one factory size still bend the usual U-shape in the short run?
steps.right: Yes, it is a normal short-run average cost curve
steps.wrong: No, it becomes flat once built
steps.hint: Even after choosing a size, the firm is still stuck with that size for a while, which is the short run.
steps.pre: Each possible factory size has its own short-run curve, called a

steps.q: The bakery could build a small, medium or large factory. Each size gives its own short-run cost curve, but the firm can only ever operate on the lowest point achievable for its current size. What does the long-run curve trace out across all these short-run curves?
steps.right: The lowest points of all the short-run curves, touching each one
steps.wrong: The highest points of all the short-run curves, avoiding each one
steps.hint: The long run is built from choosing the best short-run curve at each output.

steps.q: A firm doubles its size and now buys ingredients in bulk at a discount, and can afford specialist equipment it could not justify before. As output rises, what happens to its long-run average cost?
steps.hint: Bulk buying and better equipment tend to cut the cost per unit, not raise it.

steps.q: The firm keeps growing until it becomes so large that managers struggle to communicate, decisions slow down and coordination breaks down. As output rises further, what happens to its long-run average cost now?
steps.hint: Poor communication and slow decisions tend to push costs per unit up, not down.
